intro: Everything learned from reading all 22 H156 papers and their mark schemes side by side: how marks are actually awarded, where they are lost, and what keeps coming back. Figures update from the question data in this tool.

mechanics.title: Working earns most calculation marks
mechanics.body: Multi-step calculations are usually marked C1 C1 A1. The two C1 marks are for correct substitution, so clear working still scores 2 of 3 with a wrong final answer. A bare answer that is wrong scores nothing.
mechanics.stat: 53 of 91 multi-step parts use C1 C1 A1

mechanics.title: In a show-that, the method is the mark
mechanics.body: About half the show-that schemes give the final printed value A0. Show every substitution, then give your value to one more significant figure than printed (3.39 for 3.4, 839 for 840). Rounding to the printed value without the extra figure is the most common slip.
mechanics.stat: 27 of 55 show-that parts give the final value A0

mechanics.title: Error carried forward has limits
mechanics.body: Arithmetic slips, transcription errors and power-of-ten (POT) errors cost one mark, then later parts are marked on your wrong value (ecf). Using the wrong physics (XP), such as the wrong equation or squaring an area, is not carried forward and loses the dependent marks.
mechanics.stat: ecf is mentioned in about 100 mark-scheme notes

mechanics.title: Contradictions and hedging score zero
mechanics.body: If you write a right and a wrong statement, the mark is lost. Only the number of list items asked for is marked, in order. Two letters in a multiple-choice box score nothing.

mechanics.title: Significant figures
mechanics.body: Give 2 or 3 s.f. by default. Too few is penalised once per paper. When a question asks for a set number of s.f., the final mark needs exactly that number.
mechanics.stat: 24 parts ask for a stated number of s.f.

mechanics.title: Use g = 9.81 m s⁻²
mechanics.body: Using g = 10 is penalised wherever it changes a 2 s.f. answer, except in estimates.

mechanics.title: When a unit mark exists
mechanics.body: A unit only costs a mark when the question asks for it and the scheme has a separate unit mark (Ω m, Pa s, C, N s). If the unit is printed on the answer line you need not repeat it, but a wrong unit you add can still contradict your answer.
mechanics.stat: 6 parts carry a B1 for the unit alone

commands.need: A numerical answer with working. Show the equation, the substituted values in SI units, then the answer to sensible s.f.
Usually a value from data or a graph, or several steps. Show what you read off (draw it on the graph) and how you used it.
Every step visible, ending with your own value to more s.f. than the printed one. A missing step loses the method mark.
A chain of reasoning: cause → what changes → effect, using the physics term at each link. Count the marks: 2 marks means two linked points, 3 marks a full chain.
A short answer, no reasoning needed. Precision of the key word matters more than length.
What happens or what you would do, step by step. For practicals: apparatus, what you measure and with what, and how.
Any sensible physics-based answer is credited. Never leave it blank.
Sensible assumed values (state them), one significant figure is fine, and the order of magnitude must be right.
Shape and key features, not precision: labelled axes, correct start point, smooth line, arrows that follow round in a vector triangle, a ruled best-fit line.

practical.title: Gradients
practical.body: Draw a large triangle covering at least half your line and use points on the line, not data points. Include the axis multipliers (×10⁻³ and so on). Small triangles and single data points are rejected.

practical.title: Worst line
practical.body: Uncertainty in a gradient = |best gradient − worst gradient|. The worst line is the steepest or shallowest line through all the error bars.

practical.title: Combining uncertainties
practical.body: Add percentage uncertainties when multiplying or dividing, and multiply by the power for squares and cubes (r² doubles it). Diameter-squared terms are where this is usually tested.

practical.title: Tangents
practical.body: For a rate on a curve, draw a tangent touching at that point only, then use a large triangle on the tangent.

practical.title: Improving an experiment
practical.body: Credit goes to specific improvements tied to the stated problem: a named instrument with better resolution, repeating and averaging, a larger range, data logger or light gates for short times. 'Be more careful' scores nothing.

practical.title: Measuring small things
practical.body: Wire diameter: micrometer, several places along the wire, take the mean. Never a ruler. Length: metre rule; time: light gates or a data logger for fast events.

practical.title: Percentage difference
practical.body: Compare your value with the accepted one: |yours − accepted| / accepted × 100%. Several papers ask whether a result is 'consistent' — compare the difference with the uncertainty.

lor.summary: Each Paper 2 has two six-mark Level of Response questions, marked as a whole: the examiner picks a level (L1 1–2, L2 3–4, L3 5–6) from how complete and clear the answer is, then a mark within it.
checklist: A labelled diagram of the set-up
Named measuring instruments for every quantity
What you vary, what you measure, and what you keep constant
A safety point specific to this experiment (not 'wear goggles' unless it fits)
The straight-line graph you would plot, with axes named
How the gradient or intercept gives the answer, including any formula rearrangement
If asked, how you would get the percentage uncertainty
lor.note: Answers that describe the method well but stop before the analysis usually cap at Level 2. Explanation-style six-markers (e.g. comparing materials, explaining a phenomenon) need every term in the question defined and used.

units: A = πd²/4; halve d before using r

items: Work function and threshold frequency definitions need 'minimum'
Explain with one photon to one electron; intensity changes the number of electrons, not their energy
A wave-model explanation scores nothing
Convert eV to J before using hf = φ + KEmax
Taking a square root to get speed from KE is often forgotten
Convert nm and mW before substituting
Photon rate = power ÷ energy of one photon; don't invert it
Planck constant from LEDs: plot V against 1/λ, gradient = hc/e
Doubling frequency doubles photon energy; it does not double the number of photons
Node to node is λ/2, not λ
A closed end is a node, an open end an antinode
Explain formation by reflection and superposition of waves of the same frequency travelling in opposite directions
Fundamental in a closed tube: L = λ/4
Know the differences from progressive waves: energy transfer, amplitude and phase between points
Coherence means a constant phase difference, not 'same phase'
In λ = ax/D, x is one fringe spacing: divide the span by the number of gaps
Path difference nλ gives constructive, (n + ½)λ destructive
Phase difference is in degrees or radians as asked; check which
Angles are measured from the normal
sin C = 1/n only for light going from the denser medium into air
Above the critical angle there is no refracted ray
Polarisation: intensity falls to zero at 90°, back to maximum at 180°
Read period from a time graph and wavelength from a distance graph; don't mix them
Intensity ∝ amplitude²: doubling amplitude quadruples intensity
Phase difference = (distance ÷ λ) × 360°
Convert ms, cm and GHz
Vout = R2/(R1 + R2) × Vin with all resistances in the same unit (kΩ vs Ω)
Explain sensors in a chain: light or temperature → resistance → share of p.d. → output
Use the correct LDR and thermistor symbols
In practical answers, include calibration or a reference value
E = V + Ir: plot V against I, gradient = −r, intercept = E
Lost volts rise with current, so terminal p.d. falls
Voltmeter goes across the cell, ammeter in series
Don't forget the minus sign when reading r from the gradient
Use cross-sectional area πd²/4 with d in metres
Unit of resistivity is Ω m, not Ω m⁻¹
Measure diameter with a micrometer in several places
Plot R against L: gradient = ρ/A
I = Anev: a thinner wire means a higher drift velocity for the same current
Number density n is per m³
Conventional current is opposite to electron flow
Convert GPa and mm² before substituting
Elastic energy is the area under the force–extension graph; don't drop the ½
Young modulus is the gradient of the linear part of stress against strain
Use weight (mg) as the force, not mass
State Newton's second law as force ∝ rate of change of momentum, not F = ma alone
Opposite directions: add speeds for the change in momentum
Impulse = area under force–time graph; unit N s
Newton's third law pairs act on different objects and are the same type of force
Horizontal velocity is constant; vertical motion has g
Resolve the launch velocity: horizontal v cos θ, vertical v sin θ — don't swap them
At the top, vertical velocity is zero but KE is not
With air resistance: lower and shorter, not symmetrical
Principle of moments: sum of clockwise = sum of anticlockwise moments about any point
Moment = force × perpendicular distance
A triangle of forces must close, with arrows following round
Resolve forces; never add magnitudes of forces at an angle
Convert cm and g before using ρ = m/V
p = hρg uses depth in metres
Upthrust equals the weight of fluid displaced
A floating object: upthrust = its weight
Say u = 0 when dropped from rest
Thinking distance depends on speed and reaction time; braking distance depends on speed² and the braking force
Displacement is the area under a v–t graph; acceleration is its gradient
Use g = 9.81 m s⁻²

mcq: Answers are spread evenly across A, B, C and D, so there is no letter to guess towards.
Waves (4.4) supply the most questions, then forces in action (3.2) and circuits (4.2).
About a third are pure recall, and about a third need a quick calculation. Do the working in the margin; it takes less time than guessing wrong.
Difficulty doesn't rise through Section A, so skip and come back rather than slowing down.
Budget roughly a minute each, about 20–25 minutes for Section A.
timing: Both papers are 70 marks in 1 hour 30 minutes: about 1.3 minutes per mark. Leave 10–12 minutes for each six-mark question on Paper 2.

more.title: Graphs are everywhere
more.body: About a fifth of all question parts involve a graph: reading values, gradients, areas, plotting or sketching. Practise reading scales with multipliers and drawing large gradient triangles until it is automatic.

more.title: Bank the opening parts
more.body: The first part of each structured question is usually the easiest: a definition, a show-that or a single-step calculation. Do these fast and accurately; they fund the time for harder parts later.

more.title: Difficulty only creeps up
more.body: Section B and Paper 2 get only slightly harder towards the end. The hardest parts are the six-mark answers and long multi-step calculations, and 15 of the 72 hardest parts are an opening (a), so don't save effort for the last question.

more.title: Circuits are where hard marks hide
more.body: By our difficulty ratings, potential dividers and other circuit topics hold many of the hardest parts. The examiners' reports add a different angle: the topics most often 'poorly answered' were evaluating experiments, drag and terminal velocity, Newton's laws and momentum, moments and equilibrium, and refraction and wave basics, while circuits sat in the middle. Revise both lists.

more.title: Both papers test the same topics in the same session
more.body: In most sessions the large majority of sub-sections on Paper 2 also appear on Paper 1. Seeing a topic on Paper 1 does not mean Paper 2 will skip it, so don't revise by elimination between the papers.

more.title: Quantum links to energy and circuits
more.body: The recurring cross-topic calculations join quantum physics to earlier work: photon rate from an LED's power, photoelectron speed from kinetic energy, and de Broglie wavelength from an accelerating p.d. via eV = ½mv². Practise these chains end to end.

difficulty.name: Easy
difficulty.what: One idea, one step. Recall a definition or fact, substitute straight into a single equation, read a value off a graph, or pick a multiple-choice answer you either know or don't.
requires: Exact recall of definitions, units and standard facts
Choosing the one equation that fits and substituting correctly
Usually 1–2 marks, rarely more than one equation
difficulty.tackle: These are speed and accuracy marks. Answer briefly, use the precise key word, convert units, and move on.

difficulty.name: Standard
difficulty.what: Two or three linked steps. Combine two equations, rearrange before substituting, take a gradient and use it, explain a cause-and-effect chain, or work through an uncertainty.
requires: Rearranging and chaining two equations, carrying an intermediate value
Linking a physical change to its effect in a short explanation
Using a graph quantitatively: gradient, intercept or area
Basic uncertainty work and sensible significant figures
difficulty.tackle: Write the working as a chain so each step earns its C1 mark, and in explanations name the physics at every link.

difficulty.name: Hard
difficulty.what: Planning, judgement or synthesis. Six-mark experiment designs, multi-stage calculations that cross topics, evaluating data against a claim, sketching an unfamiliar graph, or applying ideas to a setting you haven't seen.
requires: Designing a complete method with analysis (most hard marks are six-mark answers)
Deciding the route through a problem yourself: no prompts for intermediate steps
Combining topics, e.g. quantum with energy, or circuits with materials
Judging data: consistency, uncertainty, whether a conclusion is valid
difficulty.tackle: Plan before writing. For calculations, write down what you're finding and the equation chain first. For six-markers, follow the Level 3 checklist so no strand is missed.

content.title: Recall equations
content.body: The spec says five equations must be recalled rather than looked up: F = ma, W = mg, Ek = ½mv², Ep = mgh and R = V/I. They are needed in dozens of parts, so know them cold.

content.title: Planning is never multiple choice
content.body: Experimental design (1.1.1), using apparatus (1.1.2) and circuit symbols (4.2.1) only appear in written Section B and Paper 2 parts. Practise writing methods, not just recognising them.

content.title: Diffraction gratings are a gap
content.body: The spec lists finding the wavelength of light with a diffraction grating as a technique (4.4.3(g)(ii)), but no question in any of the 22 papers has used one; every wavelength-of-light question uses a double slit. Know how the grating practical is set up and what is measured, as it is examinable.

content.title: Drag appears in a narrow way
content.body: Terminal velocity is tested through a few repeated set-ups: a ball or paper cone falling, drag proportional to v², and data-logged distance–time readings. Skydiver-style questions hardly appear.

content.title: Familiar settings recur
content.body: Balls and projectiles, sound in tubes, cars and stopping, trolleys colliding, floating objects, springs and metal plates in the photoelectric effect appear in almost every session. Unfamiliar settings are usually these same physics ideas in new clothes.

notes.title: Hard means stacking moves
notes.body: Verified by reading every part: easy written parts need 0.9 moves and about 1.3 reasoning steps on average, standard 1.4 moves and 2.2 steps, hard 2.0 moves and 3.4 steps. The physics is the same AS content; the number of linked moves is what changes.

notes.title: Explanations get harder, not easier
notes.body: Cause → effect explanations rise from 4% of easy parts to 26% of hard ones, making them the most common move in hard parts. Six-mark explanation questions and multi-link 'explain' parts are where they sit. (This corrects an earlier estimate that said explanations peaked at standard.)

notes.title: Unfamiliar formulae and planning appear almost only in hard parts
notes.body: A formula given in the question shows up in 12% of hard parts and almost never below. Planning an experiment jumps from 7% at standard to 21% at hard. Both are concentrated in Paper 2's six-mark questions.

notes.title: Linearising is rarer than it looks, but decisive
notes.body: Only about 30 parts need you to choose or interpret what to plot (15% of hard parts). Since 2022 the six-mark graph questions usually give the equation, and since 2023 often the plotted graph too, so the skill tested is interpreting the gradient and intercept rather than inventing the plot.

notes.title: The step up usually comes after part (a), but not always
notes.body: Of 72 hard parts, 25 are a (b), 15 a (c) and 11 are whole six-mark questions, but 15 are an (a). Don't assume the first part is always gentle.
